title: Temporal reuse cliffs and NVMe smoothing playbook
content:
Purpose:
This is a focused lab playbook for investigating sudden drops ("reuse cliffs") in KV-cache reuse rates that correlate with NVMe paging bursts and memory-bandwidth amplification. The goal is to capture causal signatures, measure impact on tail latency and throughput, and iterate mitigation ideas (smoothing, prefetch-policy hysteresis, NVMe QoS shims).

Background and motivation:
We have recurring customer incidents where p99+ token latency spikes during multi-tenant surges. Initial traces point to large contiguous KV misses that cause NVMe read spikes and queuing; after that, reuse falls and the working set enters a lower-residency regime (a "cliff") that takes seconds to recover. Existing notes cover eviction heuristics and hotset skew but haven't explored the transient interaction between sequence-length driven reuse and NVMe IO smoothing.

Hypotheses to test:
1) Rapid growth in long-seqlen requests causes KV lookup footprint to jump nonlinearly, producing large read batches that saturate NVMe throughput and amplify host PCIe/memory channel contention.
2) If NVMe IO is bursty, the OS/device queues add intra-request jitter which leads to misattribution in our residency telemetry (we see misses that were actually delayed reads), causing the runtime to accelerate eviction and worsen reuse.
3) Introducing a small amount of NVMe read-smoothing (rate-limiting or micro-batching with jitter) + hysteresis in eviction scoring will flatten tail latency and shorten cliff recovery time.

Experiment matrix (high level):
- Independent variables:
  - workload seqlen mix: baseline (typical mix), long-tail (20% > 2048 tokens), all-long (50% > 2048)
  - NVMe behavior: native (no shaping), shaped (pacing reads to X MB/s), aggregated micro-batch (coalesce reads within 4ms window)
  - eviction policy hysteresis: none, mild (2x grace window), strong (4x grace window)
  - KV pinning: none, hot-key pin enabled
- Metrics to collect:
  - reuse_rate(t) sampled at 100ms resolution (per-host, per-model)
  - NVMe read bandwidth & IOPS (device counters) at 100ms
  - p50/p95/p99/p999 token latency
  - spike recovery time: time to return to baseline reuse_rate after cliff
  - CPU and memory channel saturation counters (perf)

Instrumentation and data capture checklist:
- Add 100ms-resolution reuse and miss traces to telemetry; include per-key age histogram for misses.
- Capture block-level NVMe metrics (Windows: PerfMon or Linux: iostat/blktrace) and also device SMART/queue depth if available.
- Trace two types of events: "logical miss" (runtime thought miss) vs "io-completed-miss" (actual disk completion) and log timestamps for both. This lets us detect delayed read misattribution.
- Collect host-level perf counters: mem_bandwidth (bytes/s), memory controller stalls, PCIe latency counters when available.
- Synthetic client harness: generate controlled seqlen mixes. Tag requests with stable client id so we can correlate per-stream locality.

Lab harness and commands (notes):
- Use the existing microbench harness (scripts/kv_workload_driver) with options: --seqlen-mix long-tail --rps 600 --clients 40 --pin-hot 0
- Configure device shaping with blktrace + tc + dm-throttle shim or vendor-supplied nvme-cli QoS: e.g. nvme qcow2 shim for testbed. For prototype, we used fakerate: sudo ./tools/nvme-shaper --device /dev/nvme0n1 --rate-mbps 800
- Start runtime with debug flags: RUNTIME_KV_TELEMETRY_INTERVAL_MS=100 RUNTIME_EVICTION_HYSTERESIS_MS=0
- To instrument reads: enable IO hooks in runtime: KV_IO_HOOKS=1 (logs logical_miss_ts and io_complete_ts).

Representative run: baseline -> NVMe burst -> cliff -> mitigation
- Baseline: reuse_rate avg=0.62, p99 token latency=18ms
- Induce long-tail: reuse_rate drops to 0.28 within ~1.2s, NVMe bandwidth jumps from 340MB/s to sustained 1.6GB/s, device queue depth > 256, p99 jumps to 280ms, p999 > 1s
- Observed mismatch: logical_miss -> io_complete delta distribution shows bimodal peaks: fast reads (~3ms) and slow reads (~120ms) indicating queueing. Many logical misses are later marked as io-complete after the eviction pass has already demoted entries.

Results summary (initial):
- Hypothesis 1 validated: long-tail seqlen mix induces superlinear read amplification.
- Hypothesis 2 supported: the delayed-read signature correlates strongly with cliff onset; eviction code uses timestamp windows that are too short and treats delayed-but-present entries as cold.
- Hypothesis 3 promising: two mitigation primitives combined reduced p99 by ~4x in the testbed: (1) NVMe micro-batching (coalesce reads within 3-5ms) and (2) a mild eviction hysteresis (2x grace window). Recovery time dropped from ~12s to ~2.3s.

Mitigations explored (details):
1) NVMe micro-batching: aggregate small read requests for adjacent keys into a single larger read when they map to contiguous or near-contiguous NVMe LBAs. Implementation in the prototype worked by deferring reads up to W ms (configurable). Tradeoffs: small increase in read amplification if aggregation picks unrelated keys; tuning W=3ms gave best p99 reduction without increasing average latency.
2) Pacing (rate-limiting) reads: limit steady-state NVMe read rate to X MB/s so peaks are smoothed. Simple to implement via device-shaper. Too aggressive pacing increases average latency; found sweet spot at 60% of raw device bandwidth for our testbed.
3) Eviction hysteresis: when an entry is first observed as a miss, mark it pinned for an extra N ms before considering for eviction. This prevents eviction of entries that are on the way back from IO. N tuned to median delayed-read time + safety margin.
4) Prefetch with backpressure-aware windows: speculative prefetch of likely next keys but stop prefetching when NVMe queue depth hits a threshold. Prefetch lowered p50 slightly and helped p99 when combined with hysteresis.

Telemetry artifacts (examples to review):
- time-series: reuse_rate_100ms, nvme_rd_bw_100ms, device_qdepth_100ms, p99_latency_100ms
- scatter: logical_miss_delay vs device_qdepth for all miss events in window
- histogram: delta(logical_miss_ts, io_complete_ts) before vs after mitigation

Open questions and next experiments:
- Multi-tenant fairness: do micro-batching and pacing create head-of-line issues across tenants? Need cross-tenant experiments (two tenant profiles competing).
- Controller-level NVMe QoS: vendor offload (namespace QoS) vs host-level shaping—tradeoffs in latency guarantees.
- Hot-key vs locality: test if aggregation heuristics can use model-aware key ordering to improve coalescing accuracy.
- More realistic production traces: run with production RPS and request correlations to see long-term stability.

Runbook snippets for on-call (triage):
1) If p99 spikes > 200ms and device_qdepth > 200, check reuse_rate trend. If reuse falling rapidly, mark incident as "NVMe-induced reuse cliff".
2) Toggle soft mitigation: increase eviction hysteresis flag (admin toggle) and enable temporary NVMe pacing for the host; observe p99 within 30s.
3) If toggles don't help, fail over traffic to a less-bursty cluster (routing policy) and capture full traces for postmortem.

Implementation notes and risks:
- Adding read deferral (micro-batching) requires careful backpressure to avoid amplifying PCIe or memory channel saturation.
- Eviction hysteresis increases memory pressure under very high unique-key churn; must be bounded with adaptive sampling.
- Device shaping is a band-aid: production must prefer runtime-level mitigation + smarter admission rather than relying on host-level QoS for customers.

Next steps (action items):
- (Ava) Produce 3 repeatable runs with long-tail mixes and attach plots + raw telemetry to SRT-2107 by 2026-03-08.
- (Diego) Prototype a production-safe micro-batching variant that uses model-key locality hints; demo in sandbox by 2026-03-15.
- (Priya) Run cross-tenant fairness matrix and propose safe default hysteresis values by 2026-03-20.

Appendix: quick command list and scripts referenced:
- ./scripts/kv_workload_driver --profile long-tail --rps 600 --clients 40 --duration 120
- sudo ./tools/nvme-shaper --device /dev/nvme0n1 --rate-mbps 800  # prototype only
- RUNTIME_KV_TELEMETRY_INTERVAL_MS=100 RUNTIME_EVICTION_HYSTERESIS_MS=2000 ./bazel-bin/serving/runtime_server
- To capture IO pairing: cat /var/log/kv_io_hooks.log | jq -r '. | [ .logical_miss_ts, .io_complete_ts, .key ] | @tsv' > io_pairs.tsv

Notes-to-self: prioritize clarity in the telemetry naming (logical_miss vs io_complete) and push a small documented flag to allow on-call to activate hysteresis/pacing without a full deployment.

-- end of playbook --
